## Prerequisites

ENCMP 100 (or equivalent), MATH 102, MATH 201, and MATH 209, subject to confirmation against the current University Calendar.

## Course purpose

MATE 374 develops the numerical judgement needed to turn a materials question into a trustworthy computational result. Students will formulate mathematical problems, select and apply numerical methods, examine the effects of approximation and finite precision, and interpret calculations at several materials length and time scales.

Python is the main language used for small transparent calculations. Established scientific libraries and materials-simulation software are introduced where they help answer an engineering question. Programming mechanics remain subordinate to model choice, error analysis, verification, and physical interpretation.

The recurring workflow is

$$
\text{materials question}
\rightarrow
\text{model and assumptions}
\rightarrow
\text{numerical representation}
\rightarrow
\text{computation}
\rightarrow
\text{verification}
\rightarrow
\text{interpretation}.
$$

## Course learning outcomes

By the end of the course, given a materials problem, dataset, or computational result, students should be able to:

1. **Formulate** the physical question as a mathematical problem with stated variables, assumptions, scales, units, and conditions.
2. **Select** a suitable numerical method by considering the mathematical structure, required accuracy, robustness, and computational cost.
3. **Implement or inspect** core numerical procedures for scalar equations, optimization, data analysis, coupled systems, and evolution problems.
4. **Distinguish and diagnose** model-form, input, sampling, discretization, iterative, implementation, and floating-point sources of error or uncertainty.
5. **Verify** a computation using appropriate evidence such as residuals, refinement, limiting cases, conservation, units, or comparison with a reference result.
6. **Interpret** a result as a materials-engineering conclusion while stating the model's domain and limitations.
7. **Document and reproduce** a computational study using clear code, recorded inputs, software information, and an honest account of tool use.
8. **Relate** continuum, mesoscale, atomistic, and electronic simulation approaches to the questions and mathematical forms they are designed to address.

## Course organization

The course is organized around questions rather than a catalogue of software packages.

| Unit | Organizing question | Main ideas |
|---|---|---|
| Orientation and numerical thinking | Can I trust this calculation? | approximation, convergence, floating point, performance |
| Finding special points | Where is a root, equilibrium, or minimum? | bisection, fixed point, secant, Newton, optimization |
| Functions and data | What can sampled values support? | differentiation, integration, interpolation, regression |
| Coupled systems | How do several variables interact? | vectors, matrices, linear and nonlinear systems |
| Evolution in time | How does a material state change? | ODE formulation, timestep error, stability, established solvers |
| Fields and conservation | How does change move through a material? | fluxes, grids, boundary conditions, PDE discretization |
| Simulation across scales | Which representation fits the question? | phase field, Monte Carlo, MD, electronic structure, modern data-driven links |

## Learning materials and computing

The [course notes](../units/index.qmd) are the main reference and are designed for both browser reading and printing. Interactive activities use marimo notebooks in the browser where practical. Molab or another approved environment may be used for packages or hardware unavailable in browser-only Python.

Students should have regular access to a modern web browser. Device or installation difficulty should not prevent participation; static and paired routes will be provided for essential activities. Installation requirements for assessed work will be announced in advance.

### Recommended references

- J. Kiusalaas, [*Numerical Methods in Engineering with Python 3*](https://ualberta.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/view/action/uresolver.do?operation=resolveService&package_service_id=19059219040009116&institutionId=9116&customerId=9115&VE=true).
- E. Sullivan, [*Numerical Methods: An Inquiry-Based Approach with Python*](https://numericalmethodssullivan.github.io/index.html).
- J. Mmbaga, R. Hayes, K. Nandakumar, and M. Flynn, *Computational Methods for Engineers: Modeling, Algorithms and Analysis*.
- W. D. Callister Jr. and D. G. Rethwisch, *Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction*.

## Assessment

| Assessment | Weight | Working form |
|---|---:|---|
| Assignments | 20% | Five computational investigations; best four counted |
| Group project | 20% | Staged materials-simulation study and final report/artifact |
| Midterm examination | 20% | 50-minute in-class examination; tentative week of October 28 |
| Final examination | 40% | Two-hour examination scheduled by the University |
| **Total** | **100%** | |

Assignment and project briefs will state the permitted collaboration, required evidence, submission format, and rubric. Substantial computational work will normally be assessed on the formulation, method choice, verification, interpretation, and reproducibility, not only on whether code produces an output.

### Assignment timing and late work

The working plan is to release five assignments through Canvas with approximately two weeks for each. The best four grades will count. Late penalties, emergency extensions, and documentation requirements will be stated in the final approved syllabus and on each assignment brief. Students facing an emergency should contact the instructor and TA as early as reasonably possible.

### Project

Students will work in teams of approximately five on a defined materials-simulation problem. The project will use staged checkpoints so that model choice, computational progress, and verification can be reviewed before the final submission. Team formation, individual accountability, grading rules, and the final format remain to be finalized.

## Examinations and permitted resources

The working plan is for open-resource examinations. Students may consult approved course notes, their own notebooks, and named Python/API documentation. Short code completion, execution, diagnosis, and interpretation may be required.

Generative-AI and person-to-person communication will not be permitted during examinations. The final list of allowed devices, websites, local files, calculators, and software will be published before each examination and will supersede this draft.

No official formula sheet is currently planned because the examinations are open resource. Students are encouraged to build their own concise reference notes throughout the term.

## Academic integrity and AI-assisted work

Students are responsible for following the University of Alberta Student Academic Integrity Policy and for understanding the permitted collaboration stated on each assessment.

AI-assisted coding is permitted for assignments and the project unless a task explicitly states otherwise. Students remain responsible for the correctness and authorship of submitted work. They must be able to explain the model, algorithm, code, verification, and interpretation.

Any submitted work that used an AI-assisted tool must include a short disclosure naming the tool and describing its contribution. Students must not submit generated code or prose they cannot defend, fabricate results or citations, or enter confidential, personal, proprietary, or restricted data into external services.

A course-specific [Gemini assistant](https://gemini.google.com/gem/7d47e82eecb2) is available as an optional coding aid. University guidance and the assessment-specific rules still apply.

## Accommodations, illness, and missed work

Students requiring accommodations should register through the University's approved process and contact the instructor early enough to confirm that course software and resources will be accessible in the accommodated setting.

Procedures for missed term work, a missed midterm, deferred final examinations, and reappraisal will follow the final Faculty and University policy language. Contact the instructor and TA promptly when illness or an emergency affects an assessment; do not rely on this draft for a formal deadline or documentation rule.

## Respectful learning environment and recordings

The course follows University and Faculty expectations for respectful, professional, safe, and inclusive conduct. Course materials, class recordings, and student work may not be redistributed except as permitted by the University, the copyright holder, or an approved accommodation. The final syllabus will include the required Faculty policy language.
